messages.subject: koyck model in stan
parts:
Hi to everyone on the STAN users mailng list : I'll try to be brief but I wanted to explain the history of my problem first. The model I'm trying to fit is called the koyck disributed lag and has  a long classical history. In fact, it was developed in 1951
in the Ph.D thesis of Koyck. Phoebus dhrymes actually wrote a whole book on it and there have been many, many papers on it because estimating it, even classically, was not easy before computers got powerful. This is because there
are similarities between the koyck model and the GLS model ( serial correlation ) that are not necessary to go into here.

But I'm not so sure about it's history as far as bayesian attempts to estimate it. The paper that attempts to estimate it using gibbs sampling is attached but I found an error in it ( equation 44 ) and the authors don't provide the explicit GIbbs sampling
 code that estimated the model so I'm not so sure about the correctness of the results.  Also, there is definitely an issue at the boundary when rho is near 1 so that could be the reason why I have had so many problems estimating it. The beginning of attached  paper provides a discussion of the gelman-meng example and how one can get ridges in the likelihood or a bi-modal likelihood depending on the true parameter values.  The actual koyck model is discussed on pages 19-22. ( although the discussion between pages 12-18 is also quite relevant ) and pages 23-24 talked about problems at the boundary and how to deal with them.

My history with the model is that I worked on the bayesian estimation of it about 3 years ago. I made three different attempts:

1) I tried Rjags. ( I have that code if anyone is interested ).

2) I wrote my own code using gibbs sampling. When that didn't work, I wrote a metropolis hastings algoriithm. That wasn't successful either. ( I have that R code also ).

3) I tried to use the R admit package. That package generates a mixture of student t-densities as the proposal for an MH algorithm. It was actually the most successful of the three attempts but when the rho parameters was near the boundaty,
it also had problems.

The main problem is that the model I'm estimating with real data would be expected to have estimates of rho in the (0.9 - 1.0) range so having problems near the boundary is a real problem.

So, I heard about STAN a month or so ago and, after reading about HMC and NUTS, I finally tried it tonight. I didn't get good parameter estimates but of course I could be doing something incorrectly. I've only just started reading the Jags manual but this model is actually not that different from an AR(1) because a koyck distributed lag reduces to something pretty similar to an AR(1). So, the AR(1) model in the STAN manual really helped a lot. 

From reading the manual and Ben's great postings, it seems that RSTAN assumes flat improper priors for parameters that aren't explicity given a prior. So, I think the model matches what is in the paper as far as the joint prior.

Also,  I realize that it's a lot of work to look at the paper and the model etc but, if  anyone is interested, I'd really appreciate it and maybe something interesting could come out of it. I originally emailed Andrew a month or so ago about making a
contest on estimating this model on his blog but then he mentioned STAN which I had zero knowledge of.  Thanks Andrew.

As far as how my 3 years ago journey ended,  I ended up estimating the model using optimization methods but I'd love to know if it actually can be estimated using any kind of MCMC approach. Plus, when you use classical methods, you
have to decide on what time window to use to re-update the model estimates etc. A bayesian approach would avoid the need for that.

Or maybe it's a rare example of a model that just cannot be estimated using an MCMC approach. Thank you to anyone who wants to take a look. If anyone is interested, then my suggestion would be to read pages 1-22 of the attached paper. It's well written and really clear. It's only the Gibbs sampling results that I'm skeptical of. Thank you very much and if anyone has any questions about the model, feel free to ask me. Also, one more piece of info: 3 years back, I did get help from Ed Greenberg as far as asking him about my GIbbs sampling R code  and he wasn't able to figure out why my Gibbs sampling R code wasn't working so  I'm pretty certain that it's not possible to estimate it using regular GIbbs sampling.

Finally, my thanks to all of the people involved in Stan and Rstan. The instructions for getting it to run are so well written that it was a breeze. I always have bad times with software installations and, aside from my dopey locale problem, it was a piece of cake getting STAN and Rstan to work on my linux machine. Also, although I only started reading it today, the STAN manual is incredible with all the examples and details and explanations. and the users list is amazingly educational also. Thank you all  very much.


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              Mark

As an aside, if anyone knows anything that would help me understand NUTS more, please let me know. The authors, Andrew and Matt, are both well known and extremely clear in their writings but the connection between binary trees and their depth and using that information to decide when to stop the trajectory generation is something I'm just not getting.  Thanks again.

messages.subject: Re: koyck model in stan
parts: On Saturday, April 6, 2013 2:24:16 AM UTC-4, Mark Leeds wrote:

From reading the manual and Ben's great postings, it seems that RSTAN assumes flat improper priors for parameters that aren't explicity given a prior. So, I think the model matches what is in the paper as far as the joint prior.

Minor correction: The priors are uniform over their declared support, unless you bend the prior explicitly with a sampling statement in the model {} block such as beta ~ normal(0,1). But a uniform prior is proper if the support is bounded on both sides, which is the case here with rho in (0,1).

As to your model, the wall time would improve if you pulled the sampling statement out of the loop:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of data points 
  real y[N];
  real x[N];
}

model {
 real mu[N];
 mu[0] <- y[0];
for ( n in 2:N)

mu[n] ~ rho * y[n-1] + beta * (1-rho) * x[n];

 y ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

If you are quite sure that in your real example that rho is large, then you can change the lower bound of the support to .8 or so, and it will sample a bit better because the unconstrained parameter underlying rho will be closer to symmetric. Also, like Carlos said, some reasonable but weak priors would help too.

Ben

I don't know what assumptions yield that joint either. My guess is such a prior puts mass on rho outside of (-1,1) even though the model would be non-stationary.

so if I do

A) lower=0, upper=1 for rho

and

B) nothing for the others,

No, even though by "nothing" you are still doing something when you restrict sigma to be positive. Possibly if you define rho as a transformed parameter, such as tanh(theta) to be on (-1,1) or logit(theta) to be on (0,1) you could construct an improper prior for f(beta, theta, sigma).
I haven't had time to play around yet but I'd like to be exact, atleast initially, and see if I can get reasonable estimates for rho reasonably near 1.0.

I think the "near 1.0" problem is manageable. For instance, you could define rho as the transformed parameter theta^(1/K) for some theta in (0,1) and sufficiently large K, in which case theta would be sufficiently below 1.0.

Also, I'd rather not put a normal prior on beta because I basically have zero information for beta so I don't want to impose information. Same for sigma. rho has to be between 0 and 1 for stationarity ( actually -1 and + 1, but i know it's positive )

Sometimes there are situations where MCMC should work in principle without prior information but does not work in practice for particular starting values, seed, etc. So, if you just put some weak priors on things, it can work better.
so a uniform prior between 0 and 1 is fine. But , when you said (0.8,1) for rho,  that would also be true for say 0.7, 0.6 etc also, right ? Thanks a lot.

Yeah, whatever lower bound you want is fine.

Another approach would go like this

parameters {

real <lower=0, upper=1> rho;
  real <lower = 0> sigma;
real beta1mrho; // equals beta * (1 - rho)

}

I just wrote a first-order Koyck model in Stan along with
a simulator in R. It all seems to work without a hitch.
Here are the links to the code:

R Simulator:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/master/src/models/misc/garch/koyck-sim.R

Stan Model:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/master/src/models/misc/garch/koyck.stan

The model (which is very much like Mark Leeds's) is short enough to dump
out in the mail:

// geometric lag time-series (Koyck 1951)
//

data {
int<lower=0> T; // number of time points
real y[T]; // output at time t
real x[T]; // predictor for time t
}
parameters {
real alpha; // intercept
real beta; // slope
real <lower=0, upper=1> lambda; // lag
real <lower=0> sigma; // noise scale
}
model {
alpha ~ cauchy(0,5);
beta ~ cauchy(0,5);
lambda ~ uniform(0,1);
sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
for (t in 2:T)
y[t] ~ normal(alpha + beta * x[t] + lambda * y[t-1],
sigma);
}

I followed the parameterization in:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_lag

I used proper priors for everything, but fairly diffuse ones.
You could eliminate the uniform one, but having it isn't going
to slow things down noticeably.

One difference from Mike Leeds's Stan model is that I used an
intercept term alpha. Without an intercept, the outputs should
be centered (this could be done in Stan's transformed data block).

Here's the simulator in R:

library("rstan");

T <- 200;
x <- rnorm(T,0,1);
alpha <- -1.25;
beta <- 0.75;
lambda <- 0.6;
sigma <- 0.5;

y <- rep(NA,T);
y[1] <- rnorm(1,alpha + beta * x[1],sigma);
for (t in 2:T)
y[t] <- rnorm(1,alpha + beta * x[t] + lambda * y[t-1], sigma);

fit <- stan(file="koyck.stan", data=c("T","y","x"), iter=500, chains=4, fit=fit);

compiles:

Here are some initial comments/results concerning Bob's koyck model:

1) Unfortunately, the koyck model in the wiki is incorrect. They just wrote down the reduced form but in that reduced form, there should be a (1-lambda) multiplying beta. There are
two different versions  of the reduced form of the koyck distributed model but neither of them are the one in the wiki. The two forms result from the particular assumption put on the
initial error term in the long form. I generally refer to them ( in my lingo ) as the depooter model and the baltagi model ( without intercepts )

1) depooter model ( one from earlier attachment on page 19 of adl_gibbs ):   y_t = lambda* y_t-1 + beta(1-lambda)*X_t + epsilon_t ( replacing rho in the paper with lambda )

2) baltagi ( 6.10 on page 136 of attached ) : y_t = lambda*y_t-1 + beta*(1-lambda)*X_t + epsilon_t - lambda*epsilon_t-1   

I tend to work with depooter's  but I've also estimated 2) using numerical optimization in R.

Even though the wiki model doesn't match 1) or 2), I played with Bob's model in the following ways:

A) first I took alpha out and this had no negative effects. The estimates remained fine regardless of the value of lambda.

B) then I went ahead and took the model in A) and added the (1-lambda) term to the X_t term in order to make it the depooter model. This is where problems occur.  When
lambda is in the higher range, 0.7-0.95, the estimates of beta get worse as lambda gets closer to 1.0. This is because, the coefficient (1-lambda)*beta becomes less
indentifiable as lambda gets closer to 1.0 ( this is what is discussed in adl_gibbs.pdf on pages 23-24 ).  So, atleast now I know that the problem is due to the fact that lambda is involved
in both coefficients. I haven't tried centering yet  and that will be next effort but I have one sort of related question before I work on that.

In the classical formulation, ( where I estimate the model numerical using gradients or linear regression ), then if I estimated the Depooter model using Bob's original formulation
and then just divided the model beta estimate, namely beta hat,  by (1-lambda hat) to get a betastar hat, that's a legitimate "trick" to avoid dealing with the parameter being involved in both
coefficients. Bit this is only a valid "trick" when estimating it classically I think.

In the bayesian setting, that's cheating right, because the original model isn't being told that there's a (1-lambda) term on the beta being estimated in the original model ?
I just  want to make sure that doing that is illegal statistically in the bayesian formulation.  If it's legal, then I can use Bob's formulation to back out the value of beta hat
in my formulation. But that would seem illegal to me because one is making an assumption about the coeffs of the model and not telling  the model about that assumption during estimation ?
Anyway, I'm going to try that next and see what happens: Estimate the model using Bob's formulation but back out the estimate implied by my formulation and see if it's correct ?
 
Assuming that I'm correct about that being cheating, my next step after that will be centering. The Stan code and R code for the Depooter model without alpha is provided below.
I tried different "triplets of estimates" , using the same near 1.0 value of lambda each time and lowering it away from 1.0 using the next triplet to see when good estimates of beta  start to occur.
Thanks for any insights regarding my cheating question.

R CODE
#==========================================================================================================

library("rstan");

T <- 200;
x <- rnorm(T,0,1);
for (t in 2:T)

data {
  int<lower=0> T; // number of time points
  real y[T]; // output at time t
  real x[T]; // predictor for time t
}
parameters {

real beta; // slope
  real <lower=0, upper=1> lambda; // lag
  real <lower=0> sigma; // noise scale
}
model {
beta ~ cauchy(0,5);

lambda ~ uniform(0,1);
  sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
  for (t in 2:T)
y[t] ~ normal((1-lambda) * beta * x[t] + lambda * y[t-1],sigma);

}

Many of these time-series models assume that the
outputs are centered so that there's no intercept term.

Just think of basic regression. If you have

y[n] = alpha + beta * x[n] + epsilon[n]

and

epsilon[n] ~ normal(0,sigma)

then if alpha is estimated as non-zero, then the slope-only
model is going to be less effective,

y[n] = beta2 * x[n] + epsilon2[n]

and the slope beta2 won't match the original slope beta
because it needs to try to take up some of the work
formerly done by alpha. And the scale of the error
distribution for epsilon2 will be larger.

Now if you take y[n] and subtract the average value
(which is going to be alpha = mean(y) in a basic linear regression),

y2[n] <- y[n] - mean(y);

then the regression

y2[n] = beta * x[n] + epsilon[n];

I don't know what a good reference is for centering. It should
be discussed heavily within all these time series models because
they do it all the time.

There's a bit of discussion of completely standardizing
(y -> (y - mean(y))/sd(y)), which both centers and rescales.

- Bob

The issue is that you're sampling here. You can transform samples
and still get valid samples.

For example,

y ~ normal(0,1);
z <- y * sigma + mu;

z will have a normal(mu,sigma) distribution in the samples.

You can't do it the other way around
without accounting for the Jacobian. For instance, this
won't do what you expect in tems of samples for y.

z <- (y - mu) / sigma;
z ~ normal(0,1);

For this, you need to adjust for the Jacobian because the
variable being sampled (on the left of the ~) is transformed.
(It is kosher if sigma is a constant rather than another parameter,
because the log Jacobian determinant is log |1/sigma|, which is
still constant if sigma is a constant.)

In Stan, that adjustment is the following (assuming sigma is
constrained to be positive):

lp__ <- lp__ - log(sigma);

I think it is actually the opposite: when the autoregressive parameter (lambda) gets close to 1, beta needs to go to zero. Hi Bob: I don't want to comment on beta_raw because beta_raw is from a model that can't be deduced from the original koyck model. ( the long form where there are an infinite number of coefficients ).
The model in the wiki is not possible in the sense of being a model that can be obtained from a transformation of the original infinite sum formulation. That's important because the whole point of obtaining
the reduced form of koyck distributed lag is to be able to estimate the parameters in THE ORIGINAL LONG FORM OF THE MODEL. In other words, the long form is a model that captures dampening behavior where the weights of the coefficients get less and less weight the further you go back in time. But estimating that model is difficult directly. So, the koyck transformation results in the "short form" that is
much easier to estimate ( atleast classically. but you can run into problems there too if you don't use numerical optimization and gradients ).  The point I'm trying to make is that the short form of model in the wiki doesn't have a long form correspondence. It's incorrect in terms of it corresponding to anything useful from a "distributed lag" viewpoint.  Wiki's can definitely be wrong. I've seen this happen before.

So, getting back to "Depooter" koyck:

The simplistic way I see it is that   lambda going to one in the "depooter" koyck causes an "indentifiability" problem because beta*(1-lambda) gets close to zero so it's impossible to estimate beta.

but let me write here what Lennart wrote to me in an email.  I don't have a hardcopy of the email so I'll just write it. and Lennart definitely knows what he's doing so I would bet there's some validity to the following:

Quoting Lennart from May 16, 2010 in an email to Mark Leeds:

" Hi Mark: I read your email and the relevant pages in the paper by Depooter et al: I think it is the prior that causes the problems. Indeed there must be a ridge in the likelihood for rho equal to 1 which I think is
not integrable ( having integral of infinity ),  if the prior does not "correct" it. So, under the uniform prior for rho,  the posterior kernel does not correspond to a proper distribution. In other words, intuitively
stated, the "scaling  constant" should be infinity which ruins the results.

I think a regularization prior for rho such as probability(rho) ~ (1-rho hat)^2 which keeps rho somewhat away from 1, ( similar to equation (52) in Depooter et al ) would solve the problems.".

End of Quote from Lennart Hoogerheide.

It sounds like you're dramatically over-thinking HMC, so let me try to explain.

In HMC you're not sampling from your target distribution pi(q), but rather an extended distribution pi(p, q) = pi(p | q) p (q). Hamiltonian dynamics provides a Metropolis proposal for {p, q} which is accepted with the usual Metropolis acceptance procedure for the extended distribution pi(p, q).

You then get a sample from pi(q) by simply ignoring the variables p since the marginal of the extended distribution is the target distribution, \int dp pi(p, q) = pi(q) \int dp pi(p | q) = pi(q).

I haven't looked at your model in any depth, but if there is finite posterior density at rho = 1 then there will be problems sampling with HMC. The problem is that when we transform rho to an unconstrained space the boundaries go to infinity, [0, 1] -> [-inf, inf]. If the posterior density is finite at rho = 1 then it will also be finite at rho_unconstrained = inf, and Hamiltonian dynamics falls apart when the Hamiltonian is non-zero at infinity. Computationally it's easy to see why -- if the density is non-zero out there, then the chain needs to travel all the way out to infinity which would take an infinite amount of time, not to mention wreaking havoc on any numerical implementation. This is case where using bouncing to constrain variables can help, but we haven't implemented that in Stan.

-Mike

It can be confusing because of the t-subscripting but the reduced form of the koyck model ( the one being coded in STAN )  is really just a  cross sectional regression. ( although there are issues with
correlation between regressor and noise term in estimating it as a regression but I shouldn't go into that here ). I write the model for each time t below:

y_1 = lambda* y_0 + lambda((1-p)* X_1 + epsilon_1
y_2 = lambda*y_1 + lambda(1-p)* X_2 + epsilon_2
y_3 = lambda * y_2 + lambda*(1-p)*X_3  + epsilon_3
.
.
.

the subscripts are t ( as in time ) but you can really just think of them as indices. So, I just incremented the X_t's by 1 each time in the code but that's not a trend model as you see from above. Just
different X coefficients in order to see how the parameters get estimated. If there was a second index in the y vector that was indexed by t, then that would be assuming some kind of trend. 
If you want to think of above as a time series model,  you actually can think of it as an AR(1) with an exogenous coefficient but that's not really a useful way to think of it atleast in my opinion.
You can shuffle around the (X,y ) pairs in the code using "sample" in R and re-run the model and you'll see that you'll get the same estimates. I'm not sure if that explains your trend question. Let me know.

But, the true model ( what I refer to as the long form that is really the true model. short form is just a reparameterization in order to make estimation easier  ) underlying the short form above is actually a
lagged time series model but still with no time trend. Specifically:

y_t = beta*(sum from i = zero to infinity of (lambda^i *X_t-i) + epsilon_t  for every t

This is the really interesting formulation of the model and the way I like to think of it. ( I also sometimes think of it in the short form way but this one makes it more clear to me what's really happening ).

Note that It's the same model as the short form but re-written. This model captures ( or is supposed to capture anyway ) the lagged effects of X_t  on y_t over time. So, for example, say you had a shock X_t at time t where X_t was an abundance of dollars spent on advertising at time t. ( company is doing a special advertising push say at time t ). Also, suppose you let y_t denotes sales at time t. Then what this model tries to do is capture the lagged effect of this $ investment as time goes forward from time t. Since the weights are decaying as you go firhter back in time, it's assumes that as you go back further in time,
the effect on y_t decreases. So, it's kind of like a decreasing momentum model. But it's neat because most econometric/time series models don't handle effects that occur over time. They assume the effect is all at once.

It sounds like you're dramatically over-thinking HMC, so let me try to explain.

In HMC you're not sampling from your target distribution pi(q), but rather an extended distribution pi(p, q) = pi(p | q) p (q).  Hamiltonian dynamics provides a Metropolis proposal for {p, q} which is accepted with the usual Metropolis acceptance procedure for the extended distribution pi(p, q).  
 
You then get a sample from pi(q) by simply ignoring the variables p since the marginal of the extended distribution is the target distribution, \int dp pi(p, q) = pi(q) \int dp pi(p | q) = pi(q).

I haven't looked at your model in any depth, but if there is finite posterior density at rho = 1 then there will be problems sampling with HMC.  The problem is that when we transform rho to an unconstrained space the boundaries go to infinity, [0, 1] -> [-inf, inf].  If the posterior density is finite at rho = 1 then it will also be finite at rho_unconstrained = inf, and Hamiltonian dynamics falls apart when the Hamiltonian is non-zero at infinity.  Computationally it's easy to see why -- if the density is non-zero out there, then the chain needs to travel all the way out to infinity which would take an infinite amount of time, not to mention wreaking havoc on any numerical implementation.  This is case where using bouncing to constrain variables can help, but we haven't implemented that in Stan.

-Mike

p(p,q) is a density that was defined (nor derived) by
the inventors of HMC. Among other properties, the
definition has these pleasing features:

1. The marginal density p(q) of the position q is the
distribution we want to sample from (by construction).
So if we can sample (p,q) from p(p,q), we can sample q
from p(q).

2. The joint density p(p,q) decomposes into a separable
Hamiltonian form.

In other words, my question is,

> I'll just accept it ( no pun intended ). I ask this because I don't see it all.

> distributed

These are almost always modeling assumptions, which need
to be checked.

> ... is it the discretization of the hamiltonian equations that makes one
> need the acceptance step.

Yes. If we could do the integral corresponding to the Hamiltonian
dynamics perfectly, the acceptance rate would be 100%.

The key to understanding why it maintains detailed balance is due
to volume preservation (this is the part that was tricky for me
to understand).

- Bob

On Saturday, April 13, 2013 2:11:16 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:


On 4/13/13 8:18 AM, Mark Leeds wrote:
...
> But, when I read Radford Neal's material, I must be missing some kind of key relationship between the hamilton
> equations/leapfrog steps and the probabilities. How can one just out
> of the seemingly  blue say that Prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) +K(p)]. Is that some kind of physical relationship implied
> by the hamiltonian equations themselves ?

p(p,q) is a density that was defined (nor derived) by
the inventors of HMC.  Among other properties, the
definition has these pleasing features:

   1.  The marginal density p(q) of the position q is the
       distribution  we want to sample from (by construction).
       So if we can sample (p,q) from p(p,q), we can sample q
       from p(q).

   2.  The joint density p(p,q) decomposes into a separable
       Hamiltonian form.

In other words, my question is,
> do the hamiltonian equations somehow make that relation be true ? that prob(p,q) = e to the -[U(q) + K(p)]. If so, then
> I'll just accept it ( no pun intended ). I ask this because I don't see it all.

> In statistics, one will just out of the blue say that such and such variable X is exponentially distributed or gamma
> distributed

These are almost always modeling assumptions, which need
to be checked.

> ... is it the discretization of the hamiltonian equations that makes one
> need the acceptance step.

Yes.  If we could do the integral corresponding to the Hamiltonian
dynamics perfectly, the acceptance rate would be 100%.

The key to understanding why it maintains detailed balance is due
to volume preservation (this is the part that was tricky for me
to understand).

- Bob
